newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: FEATURE-Nicaraguan land dispute divides nation.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Nicaraguan land dispute divides nation.

text.p: Udo Torres says the 690-acre (280-hectare) Hacienda Dolores coffee farm belongs to his family, who worked the land before the 1979 Sandinista revolution.

But a 75-family cooperative says it belongs to them, basing their claim on property titles given them under the agrarian reform carried out by the left-wing Sandinista government between 1979 and 1990.
And, further complicating matters, coffee company Agricris S.A. also claims a part of Hacienda Dolores that it says it bought from the cooperative.

Recently, the Torres family got a court order to evict the families from Hacienda Dolores, located 100 miles (160 kms) north of Managua in the department of Jinotega. But members of the cooperative blocked the main roads to the farm to prevent the eviction, creating an ongoing stalemate that threatened to explode into violence.
"Nobody's going to evict us from here," Pablo Francisco Vasquez, president of the Ramiro Lopez Cooperative, told the local newspaper La Tribuna.
So who is the true owner of Hacienda Dolores?

The same question hangs over about 2.5 million acres (1 million hectares) of land divvied up during the Sandinista agrarian reform, pitting former and current occupants in a bitter confrontation that threatens Nicaragua's political and economic stability.
"For Nicaragua to take-off economically, the property problem must be resolved and a state of law created," President Arnoldo Aleman told reporters recently.
WARNING OF 'TOTAL WAR' ISSUED

In the past few months, two people have been killed in violent court-ordered evictions of families who received confiscated property during the Sandinista years. Former Sandinista President Daniel Ortega called on occupants to resist evictions and added during a recent news conference:

"The war over property has started here. Blood has started to flow. If the government and its legislators in the National Assembly do not pass a law that suspends these evictions it will be a declaration of total war."

Aleman's right-wing government, which took power on Jan. 10, has made resolving the property dispute a top priority and on Jan. 27 it began negotiations with the Sandinistas. But the talks broke off at the end of February, deadlocked over the government's demand that the Sandinista party return or pay for all confiscated property in its hands and Sandinista charges that the government planned to reverse the agrarian reform and evict thousands of farmers from their land.

Ortega has demanded that the government pass a law temporarily suspending the wave of court-ordered evictions until the basic issue has been resolved as a condition for re-starting the talks. No date has been set for the talks and members of Nicaragua's business community said failure to resolve the dispute would be disastrous.
FUNDAMENTAL FOR ECONOMIC GROWTH

"A resolution to the property problem is fundamental for Nicaragua's economic growth. Without a clear respect for private property and political stability there will be little investment in Nicaragua," Gerardo Salinas, president of Nicaragua's Superior Council of Private Enterprise, said.
The issue of who owns what in Nicaragua is a problem of vast proportions.

According to a 1996 study by U.S. economist John Strasma, a professor at the University of Wisconsin, the property problem affects more than 200,000 Nicaraguan families and was the principal cause of the country's low economic production.

A survey of 6,552 coffee growers by the Coffee Growers Association of Jinotega showed that only 45 had legally valid titles to their farms. "This insecurity leads to a lack of investment, the sale of properties at bad prices and a fear by buyers to invest" in Nicaragua, Strasma's report said.
The government's official position is that it will give legal titles to poor people who received small confiscated urban and rural lots, while compensating the former owners.
But Aleman said he will make wealthy Sandinistas who received confiscated properties, and the party itself, return or pay market value for what they received.
